title: Is there life in MaaS? Why mobility-as-a-feature offers hope of revival
text:
Is there life in MaaS? Why mobility-as-a-feature offers hope of revival

# Is there life in MaaS? Why mobility-as-a-feature offers hope of revival

 Paul Halford 

 Published: 14 September 2026 

 

Whim – the first commercial application of MaaS – was first deployed in Finland to present an alternative to owning a car (pic credit: Mistervlad/Shutterstock)

Mobility as a service (MaaS) promised to transform how people travel, but its subscription model has struggled to deliver. Now, mobility-as-a-feature has been proposed as a different approach to integrating transport

Contents

- The history of MaaS
- Whim’s demise
- In defence of MaaS
- CfBT view
- ‘Mobility-as-a-feature’ comes to the fore

“I would love to drive a stake into the heart of this zombie concept,” says Thomas Ableman, the founder of Freewheeling and former Director of Strategy and Innovation at Transport for London at the government’s inquiry into integrated transport earlier this year. His impassioned, well-informed rant about mobility-as-a-service (MaaS) ends with: “Please stop talking about MaaS for ever, everyone!”

Sorry, Thomas, but we are going to talk about MaaS. routeone has, in fact, written about it several times over the years. But why has the four-letter word been so controversial, why does Thomas want the concept buried, and is it dead or simply ready for an evolution?

### The history of MaaS

MaaS is essentially traced back to around 2014, although aspects of the idea surfaced earlier. Finnish entrepreneur Sampo Hietanen, who in 2015 founded Whim – generally considered to be the first commercial MaaS supplier – described it as “a mobility distribution model in which a customer’s major transportation needs are met over one interface and are offered by a service provider”.

Put more simply, one service provider caters for all your transport needs. So, whether you use bus, car, train, micromobility or taxi, the transport is planned, accessed and paid for using a single platform. Whim was ambitiously based on a subscription model, although the overall concept can vary from that.

Why it is relevant to the coach and bus sectors is that MaaS was put forward as providing an alternative to the car but without the loss of freedom. While individual transport forms cannot compete with the car for the ultimate in independence, a package of modes stood a chance. A platform could also move someone onto a coach or bus who previously may not have considered that option.

> Please stop talking about MaaS for ever, everyone!

However, talking about Whim and its subscription model, Thomas says at the inquiry: “It was a really interesting idea but it did not work.”

He expands: “Everyone just used lots of taxis, which have a unit cost and so you cannot just have one subscription price. So they then said, ‘Oh well, never mind, we will take taxis and things that have a unit cost out, so it will just be buses and trains.’ Then everyone said, ‘Oh, you just reinvented the season ticket.’ So he said, ‘Ah no, but it’s got an app.’ Okay, so there is an app for checking information and buying tickets, which is kind of where it has landed.”

He adds that such apps make good business sense but reasons that, after 12 years, we are still waiting “for the MaaS fairies to come and solve our problems instead of just getting on with the normal day-to-day business of government fixing the framework, the targets and the incentives, and local areas getting on with delivering the data, the apps and the integration to make it work.”

Just after his Parliament critique, Thomas writes on his Freewheeling blog that “MaaS is (when taken literally) flawed and (when re-defined, as it often is) a distraction”. He compares it to software-as-a-service (SaaS), such as Netflix, where one monthly subscription gives you unlimited viewing. SaaS works, he says, because serving additional users costs virtually nothing. However, he adds that transport rarely works like that and that, if people are incentivised to use a particular mode more than they would have, the cost could substantially increase.

### Whim’s demise

The company behind Whim filed for bankruptcy in 2024, but Sampo has since defended the core concept, although he admits the business got some things wrong and that he knew at the time of founding it could be too soon for the idea to work.

Talking to routeone in June, the man who has been labelled the “father of MaaS” says Whim failed due to a combination of the COVID pandemic, the financial crisis following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and a lack of the stable government regulation required for businesses to invest in a mass market.

### In defence of MaaS

Sampo can see the argument in the Netflix analogy, but points out a difference: “If we look at Netflix or anything like that, they are in the range of tens of euros a month, whereas in mobility, the cost of a car on average in Europe is way above €600 a month, which means that it’s a completely different category.”

He adds: “If you can place yourself in the same value range or price perception of the car, you’re in a relatively high average-revenue-per-user business.”

He admits that getting people to commit to such a fee would require “perks” and “credibility”, but he adds that what people like about the car is the “certainty” that MaaS could in theory also provide.

In a MaaS model, users have to be nudged towards low-cost modes such as e-scooters, it is argued (pic credit: Raymond Orton/Shutterstock)

Within such models, he adds, various methods exist to shift people away from using those high-cost modes such as car and taxi and towards the lower-cost modes such as buses, e-scooters and e-bikes. That might be, for example, making the subscription based on “50kg of CO2 per month”, he says. Further, the Whim model offered differing layers of service which would nudge users into those more sustainable modes – for example, by limiting taxi journeys or charging extra to allow use of a rental car at the weekends.

With regards to Thomas’s complaint that Whim users “just used lots of taxis”, data from the company behind the platform, MaaS Global, shows subscribers did indeed use that mode 2.4 times as frequently than a typical Helsinki resident. However, the taxi journeys were limited to 5km and the data showed that taxi trips were frequently combined with public transport, suggesting that taxis were often being used to provide first- and last-mile connections.

Given that the data is from 2018, however, it is reasonable to ask whether the much greater availability of e-bikes and e-scooters today could take a greater share of those first- and last-mile journeys.

### CfBT view

Michael Solomon Williams, Head of Campaigns and External Affairs at Campaign for Better Transport, was also part of the panel when Thomas made those comments.

On the topic of whether MaaS could be made to work, he tells routeone: “Our inclination from Campaign for Better Transport’s perspective is that so much progress has been made on integrated multimodal ticketing and indeed there are independent apps and so forth that are doing their own ticketing offers, which could be called mobility-as-a-service.

“But I think probably I would agree with Thomas’s view that, as a concept, as a name, the public won’t think about it. As an industry, we have been thinking about it, but it’s really happening. If you’ve got integrated heavy rail, tram, bus, what’s left? Your taxi, your cargo bike, your DRT (demand-responsive transport). It’s only one final piece in the jigsaw, so I think it’s probably best left to local leaders actually to look at the integrated networks and say, we’ll do this add-on, we can bring your taxi or your DRT and include it in our integrated ticketing offer.

“But I think I would be inclined to think that MaaS as a concept doesn’t need too much focus anymore because it’s kind of happening.”

### ‘Mobility-as-a-feature’ comes to the fore

Sampo has suggested that MaaS needs to evolve into something that he and University of Sydney Business School academics call “mobility-as-a-feature” (MaaF). In a paper published in March in Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice, David A. Hensher, John D. Nelson et al. note, “We have very little to show in terms of [MaaS’s] influence on travel behaviour aligned with sustainability goals or even a business case without an injection of significant government subsidy or private venture capital”.

However, in describing MaaF, the researchers add that the “future of MaaS resides in a greater involvement of non-mobility service providers (NMSPs)”. They write: “The starting position is not with transport service providers but with organisations that, through existing or new initiatives associated with stakeholders, can offer up benefits (financial or non-financial rewards) that align with the sustainable outcome of changing traveller behaviour towards greener choices.”

Under the MaaF idea, hotels would sell you not just the room but the discounted bus ticket to get you there (pic credit: D MacDonald/Shutterstock)

Examples of MaaF already exist to some degree. Employers could provide subsidised bus or rail travel, cycling incentives or EV charging. Another example is an insurance company that, as a perk, offers discounts on public transport and micromobility options, incentives for reducing car mileage or car rental access. A hotel, instead of selling you just the room, could also sell you the sustainable transport to reach it. Or a ticket for an event could come with a free bus ticket. Owners of a residential development could offer public transport and e-bike access.

> We have very little to show in terms of [MaaS’s] influence on travel behaviour aligned with sustainability goals

Sampo himself says that MaaF would be “enabled through MaaS technology”. The cost of transport would largely be shouldered by the NMSPs.

Even if the original concept of MaaS is to be described as dead, the underlying ambition is not. Many of the concepts associated with MaaS exist in practice, but Thomas is perhaps correct that over-emphasis on it could be a distraction from simply making public transport better and more integrated.

In MaaF, MaaS may have found a way to live on. Where MaaS has struggled commercially, MaaF attempts to address that problem by putting mobility inside products that already have a business case. Perhaps MaaS does not need to be killed off but re-invented.
